<![CDATA[ <p>I wrote much of this back in 2023 and 2024 while <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> was still being implemented / was newly released. Since I began digitally scribbling my thoughts down, others ended up writing about the attribute - which was one of the reasons I didn’t feel any urgency in publishing my own post. Though, I did co-author one of <a href="https://hidde.blog/popover-accessibility/">Hidde de Vries’s articles about <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code></a>.</p> <p>But I decided to finally get this post in a publishable state because I still see people asking questions about <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code>. Like, what is it? How does it differ from a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> (modal or non)? Why doesn’t it do this one thing that I need it to? I’m not going to answer every question about <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code>. But I should get back into the habit of writing this stuff down once and pointing people to it, rather than providing repetitive one-off answers whenever I happen across someone asking about it.</p> <p>Here we (finally) go.</p> <h2 id="like-a-baked-good-a-popover-rise">Like a baked good, a popover rise</h2> <p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> attribute <a href="https://open-ui.org/components/popover.research.explainer/">was initially proposed by Open UI</a>. It does a lot for you in terms of not having to wrangle with CSS overflows or z-index clashes for your popover component. Additionally, it can provide some very handy basic focus management and dismissing behaviors. It even takes care of common accessibility mappings expected of popovers (again, read the article <a href="https://hidde.blog/popover-accessibility/">Hidde and I wrote</a>).</p> <p>But <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> by itself doesn’t do everything you may need for fully accessible custom popovers. It wasn’t meant to, nor should it. There are variations in behavior for common popovers like menus or listboxes, sub-navigation lists of links, tooltips, teaching tips, info balloons, dropdowns (<a href="https://adrianroselli.com/2020/03/stop-using-drop-down.html">whatever the hell that means</a>), light-dismissible dialogs, and [insert other made up terms for content that shows/hides while appearing atop other content].</p> <p>The tldr; is that <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> doesn’t do everything you might want it to, and that’s on purpose. Just like it’s on purpose that I’m going to be using specific quotes from Fight Club for the headings of this blog post - not every quote/heading. Just the ones that fit how I wanted to introduce new topics.</p> <h2 id="its-only-after-weve-lost-everything-were-free-to-do-anything">It’s only after we’ve lost everything we’re free to do anything</h2> <p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> attribute is a global attribute, meaning it can be used on any HTML element. That doesn’t mean you should. I mean, unless you want to create some broken crap.</p> <p>Similarly to how the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">title</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">tabindex</code> attributes are global attributes. If you put those on whatever you want without thinking of the UX / accessibility implications, then you’re likely making some janky web interfaces. Same with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code>. Declaring the attribute on arbitrary containers, without understanding the actual experience you’re making for users, is unlikely to end well for users. Particularly because unless purposefully implemented to behave as expected (based on the visual representation / content of the popover) the popover will not come with all of the necessary accessibility semantics, or keyboard functionality users might expect.</p> <p>To provide some context for the various reasons why more “automatic” accessibility semantics and keyboard functionality weren’t included, some background on the creation of the attribute is in order.</p> <h3 id="i-am-popups-broken-heart">I am <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><popup></code>’s broken heart</h3> <p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> attribute wasn’t an attribute to start. There was a proposal for a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><popup></code> element. However, when it came time to explain the semantics of the proposed element… well… it was like a non-modal dialog, but also it needed to behave like a tooltip, or popup pickers for comboboxes and menus. It could also be a popup list of sub-navigation links. But also, maybe it was even an element to be used as a generic container of content, so that content could simply be displayed above other content, without having to fight with overflow or z-index issues.</p> <p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><popup></code> element wasn’t just one thing, it was many ideas and potential use cases trying to be solved with a single element. Mind you, a single element that would not even necessarily be usable in all the contexts it could be needed, unless the HTML parser rules were changed to account for this new element. But, the level of effort to do that was not small. Nor did it help that identifying the exact semantics and a11y mappings for the element was like trying to nail mayonnaise to a rock with a deflated balloon hammer. Enjoy that mental image.</p> <p>However, outside of defining the specific semantics of the element, a native “popup” HTML feature still made sense. None of the potential use cases nor initial rational for making it an element was “bad” by any means. There were a lot of very smart people working on this proposal that all had excellent intentions. But it did not have a clear path to get accepted as a new HTML element. It did not help its case that as an element, it would have required authors to specify the necessary ARIA roles to it for most use cases. HTML did not want or need another generic <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">span</code> element. Especially since that wouldn’t be accurate if it were to then also have these special popup behaviors.</p> <p>So with the element pathway running too short for successful takeoff, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><popup></code> was given a hard critique. In doing so, it was determined that what this “element” really represented was a collection of overlapping behaviors that many different types of web “popups” needed.</p> <p>Accepting this shifted the proposal to defining a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popup</code> global attribute (which then had to be renamed to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code>, because enough web developers out there figured “why should <em>I</em> have to validate my HTML by putting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">data-</code> in front of my custom <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popup</code> attribute? What could possibly go wrong aside from preventing the standardization of a potential <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popup</code> attribute. LOL not my problem!”</p> <p>That’s right - if one decides they don’t need to add <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">data-</code> in front of their custom attribute because why do that tiny bit of extra work, it increases the potential that a new attribute will need to be named after a breakfast food. Enjoy sounding like a weirdo when talking to your non-web dev friends when you tell them how you implemented the new pastry attribute into your project.</p> <h3 id="i-am-a-global-attributes-complete-lack-of-surprise">I am a global attribute’s complete lack of surprise</h3> <p>Back to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> as a global attribute… as mentioned there are a number of instances where one would want to display certain types of content atop other content of the page. For instance:</p> <ul> <li>a sidebar navigation that “slides out” (shows/hides) and overlays some content of the page</li> <li>or more simply, a sub-navigation list of links (a “drop down”) from a persistent navigation</li> <li>a custom tooltip so you can explain information that your design and content isn’t adequately relaying on its own</li> <li>teaching tips (non-modal dialogs) that <em>should</em> be positioned in the DOM near the content they are describing</li> <li>custom combobox and menu popups (listbox, dialog or grid roles for the former, and a menu role for the latter)</li> <li>and other examples, but this list is long enough!</li> </ul> <p>There exist some HTML elements (e.g., <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">nav</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ul</code>) that already provide the accessibility semantics we need to indicate to users the type of content they’d be interacting with. But, then there are all the other types of popups/popovers that (still) don’t have native HTML equivalents. Those would need to allow <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> to be specified on things like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code> or custom elements (both <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">role=generic</code> by default) so that people could then use ARIA and additional scripting to build what they needed.</p> <p>To allow for all the known instances of where <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> could be useful, and so as to not prevent future legitimate use cases, it just made more sense to make <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> global. Though as previously mentioned, while <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> is a global attribute it doesn’t actually make sense to use it on all elements.</p> <p>For instance, declaring <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> on the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">body</code> of your web page won’t do anything you’d probably want. That is, unless your goal was to make your entire web page hidden by default. In which case, good on you I guess?</p> <p>But then there are the other elements like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">cite</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">s</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">blockquote</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ruby</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">meta</code>… take your pick really. The use cases for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> on those elements without any extra accessibility and UX considerations (or considering elements like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">meta</code> are hidden by default - LOL) are rather dubious, IMO.</p> <p>The point is that <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> can be used on any HTML element, but the intent as with any HTML feature is that developers are using the attribute and element pairing because they have a good reason. And that they are doing what is <em>necessary</em> to make their popovers accessible. That is, beyond what the browser provides, since simply declaring <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> on an element allows the browser to handle some of the (hard) work that needs doing. It’s on you to do the rest for your specific use case.</p> <h2 id="i-am-a-popovers-medulla-oblongata">I am a popover’s medulla oblongata</h2> <p>The default behaviors for the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> attribute were chosen (I dare say carefully, and often with debate and compromise) based on the common overlapping behaviors amongst various different types of researched popups. As mentioned at the start of this post, there are existing articles written about those behaviors. So, outside of briefly mentioning them, I’m going to largely focus on the stuff that was purposefully left out, and <a href="https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1047">might make people wonder why</a>.</p> <h3 id="i-am-a-popovers-overwhelming-sense-of-inadequacy">I am a popover’s overwhelming sense of inadequacy</h3> <p>Presently there are two types of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code>s, with a 3rd - ‘hint’ - only available in Chromium browsers, at the time of this writing. I’m not going to talk about hint right now, other than to say it’s primary purpose will be to create hint-like popups - e.g., tooltips and maybe even browser error messages for form fields… <em>maybe</em>.</p> <p>There is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover=manual</code> which, outside of rendering the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> in the top layer and providing the necessary accessibility mappings / tab order updating between it and its invoking button element, all other behaviors are left up to the developer to implement.</p> <p>Those other behaviors - if they are so desired, well they come with the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">auto</code> state of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover=""</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover=auto</code>). This is the type of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> that many people have veered towards, since it has additional light dismiss for mouse clicks outside of the popover and can be dismissed by use of the <kbd>Escape</kbd> key, and even TalkBack’s back gesture (in Chrome). For <kbd>Escape</kbd> key specifically, if keyboard focus is within the popover, focus will return to the invoking button - and if keyboard focus is outside of the popover, then it’ll simply close the popover.</p> <p>For the third time now, you can read more about the <a href="https://hidde.blog/popover-accessibility">accessibility of popover</a> in that other post :)</p> <h4 id="i-am-a-developers-inflamed-sense-of-rejection">I am a developer’s inflamed sense of rejection</h4> <p>There are a few things <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> in any state doesn’t do, on purpose…</p> <h5 id="keyboard-focus-doesnt-automatically-move-to-the-popover-when-it-is-invoked">keyboard focus doesn’t automatically move to the popover when it is invoked</h5> <p>Well that is unless the element used to make the popover is a dialog. Not all popovers need focus to move to them when invoked - some of them (again think tooltips or toggle tips) typically shouldn’t receive focus at all, especially if they contain no focusable elements.</p> <p>If you want focus to automatically move to your invoked popover, declare the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">autofocus</code> attribute on the element that should receive immediate and initial focus. No jS solution, buddy!</p> <h5 id="popovers-do-not-auto-dismiss-light-dismiss-when-focus-leaves-them">Popovers do not auto-dismiss (light dismiss) when focus leaves them</h5> <p>People keep wondering about this. At one point this behavior was almost a default. But upon further review and as more people outside of Open UI got involved thoughts on this matter changed (IMO, for the better).</p> <p>The light dismiss on focus out was identified as a concern due to that fact there are <em>some</em> popups on the web that do have an expectation for auto-dismiss behavior on focus out (e.g., listbox popups or menus). But since popups could be <em>any</em> type of element, e.g., non-modal dialogs or persistent popup-discloure widgets, that not all popovers should have this behavior, and that making it apply to all popovers could result in unneeded frustration for people using screen readers who might leave a popover without realizing. That could then fire a focus event on a new element outside of the popover, and then the content they were trying to review was hidden and they’d have to figure out why and re-locate the triggering element to reopen the popover and hopefully not repeat the unwanted behavior.</p> <p>On the flip side, the light dismiss via mouse/pointer event was deemed less problematic, as though people could still accidentally dismiss by errant clicking, if those people can see the screen they’d be more likely to notice the dismissal of the popover.</p> <p>Of course the “problem” with this default behavior is that some types of popovers (e.g, a select’s listbox popup and other form control ‘pickers’) do dismisses on focus leaving (hence why people should want to do this, when appropriate).</p> <p>The short of it though is that adding focus-out dismissal is far more trivial than trying to prevent the auto-dismissing if it were the default behavior. Again, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> is not meant to solve for every behavior/problem one might have. I’ll be saying this a lot. It’s kind of the point of this whole thing.</p> <h5 id="popovers-are-not-fing-modal-dialogs">Popovers are not f#&@ing modal dialogs</h5> <p>Well, at least not without some very specific effort to make sure you aren’t just making something that “looks” like it should be modal, but isn’t really. You know, one of the primary accessibility problems with many custom modal dialogs.</p> <p>Maybe it was a mistake to have a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">::backdrop</code> for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> - it seemed like there could be some potential use cases at the time. But a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> even when used on a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element, is not modal. There are a bunch of truly unfortunate, I’d even say shitty, demos out there that might make you think otherwise.</p> <p>A <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> was never meant to be modal. There is already the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element which can be shown as modal - and with the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/command-and-commandfor">command and commandfor attributes</a> one will be able to invoke a modal dialog without needing a line of JavaScript.</p> <p>Hopefully new features like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">command</code>, and <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5097714453577728"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">closedby</code></a> for dialogs (which can be used to add outside click light dismiss for modal dialogs) will help people pick the right markup for the features they’re trying to create.</p> <h5 id="a-popover-can-only-be-invoked-by-a-button-element">A <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> can only be invoked by a button element</h5> <p>Declaratively, yes. Button elements (both <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">input</code> buttons) made the most sense as the initial element to support invoking a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> - because it’s the primary use case. Button make thing go show, or hide, or both.</p> <p>A <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> also supports exposing an expanded and collapsed state, and as generic buttons don’t have any implicit behavior - declaratively marking up one to invoke a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> wouldn’t conflict with any existing behavior (which is why buttons in the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">submit</code> state don’t work with popovers when used within a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">form</code> element - because opening a popover and submitting a form have conflicting behavior).</p> <p>This decision has resulted in some jibber jabber from those who want to make custom elements or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div role=button</code> triggers for popover elements. The current solution though is to use the Popover API if one is going to be creating custom components that are already using JS anyway to recreate button elements.</p> <p>Remember, declaring an ARIA role only changes the exposed <strong>role</strong> semantics for an element - but does nothing to change the actual functionality of an element. So just like how <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div role=image alt=foo></code> doesn’t work to provide alternative text to the faux image (because <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">alt</code> is not a supported attribute for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code>) neither is simply adding <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">role=button</code> to any old element actually a solution to make <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popovertarget</code> work with that element. Doing so would fundamentally break the baseline that ARIA does not change the underlying behavior/semantics of an element.</p> <p>However, there is talk about making popovers work with custom elements which have properly set <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">elementInternals</code> to expose them as buttons. More on that some other time… For now, if you have a use case for controlling a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> with an element that isn’t a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code>, you’re going to need a smidge of JS.</p> <h5 id="tabbing-order-may-be-revised-for-popovers-but-not-the-a11y-tree">Tabbing order may be revised for popovers, but not the a11y tree</h5> <p>Something that is not always communicated in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> example posts, is that for most cases a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> and its invoking button should be siblings.</p> <p>One of the goals of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> and it rendering in the browser’s top layer was because of the hacks people needed to perform with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">z-index</code> and DOM placement, so that popups could be properly displayed above other content and not be clipped by overflowing containers.</p> <p>Top layer rendering mitigates these issues, which means that one <strong>should</strong> be able to declare their invoking element and popovers like so:</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><button</span> <span class="na">popovertarget=</span><span class="s">foo</span><span class="nt">></span>...<span class="nt"></button></span> <span class="nt"><ul</span> <span class="na">id=</span><span class="s">foo</span><span class="nt">></span>...<span class="nt"></ul></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>The reality though is that even with top layer rendering, this ideal sibling markup isn’t always going to be possible. For instance, one cannot markup an HTML list within a paragraph. Not without the browser’s parser splitting that content apart.</p> <p>So, per the following example, the tab focus reordering for popover is beneficial for keyboard users, as the hyperlink that would otherwise come between the invoking element and its popover is temporarily “skipped” when the popover is open - instead being the next tabbable element <em>after</em> the popover’s tabbable decendants.</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><p></span> I am <span class="nt"><button</span> <span class="na">popovertarget=</span><span class="s">f</span><span class="nt">></span>jack's<span class="nt"></button></span> <span class="nt"><a</span> <span class="na">href=</span><span class="s">...</span><span class="nt">></span>tabbing<span class="nt"></a></span> popover example. <span class="nt"></p></span> <span class="nt"><div</span> <span class="na">role=</span><span class="s">"[whatever is appropriate]"</span> <span class="na">popover</span> <span class="na">id=</span><span class="s">f</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="c"><!-- static content --></span> <span class="nt"><button></span>whatever i may be<span class="nt"></button></span> <span class="nt"></div></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>While browsers revise the tabbing order here so tabbing would go from the button in the paragraph, to the button in the dialog and <em>then</em> to the hyperlink, the accessibility tree is not altered. Someone using a screen reader’s virtual cursor navigation, instead of the tab key, would encounter the invoking button, the hyperlink (and any other content preceding the popover) and then the popover/its content.</p> <p>Revising the a11y tree to mitigate this is not without performance costs, and is not something that one might want a browser to even do by default for all popovers. Rather, this was determined to be something that web authors should use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">aria-owns</code> for when it would be appropriate to do so.</p> <h2 id="its-called-a-changeover-the-blog-post-goes-on-and-nobody-in-the-audience-has-any-idea">It’s called a changeover. The blog post goes on, and nobody in the audience has any idea</h2> <p>I’m not going to lie - one of the reasons I sat on this blog post for so long was because while I wanted to talk about the ins-outs of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code>, I didn’t have a neat little way to package this all up to be like “and everything’s ok! All you have to do is X to make accessible popovers! HTML gives you everything for free!”</p> <p>I don’t really care that I can’t do that, now. That’s not how this post is ending. Time to reiterate and restate.</p> <p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> attribute isn’t meant to be the end-goal. It represents a collection of behaviors that can be used to make the basis of most types of popups - including the listbox popup for the customizable select element. But, it doesn’t do everything because it shouldn’t. There are still things that people will want to do with popover which will need JS (good thing there’s also a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> API!). There are still features that are missing from/would be nice to add to HTML, there are still components that need to be built - and be accessible - and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> isn’t going to magically make them all possible without extra effort.</p> <p>But that’s not to say the book is closed on what <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> and its related attributes (and now command attributes) should be able to do. New use cases can be proposed to extend current <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">popover</code> functionality. It’s a lot easier to add new good ideas than it is to remove bad ones (I’m looking at you details/summary and your allowance of nested input elements…). If those sorts of decisions get implemented, it puts the web into an awkward place. Behavior/allowances can’t be undone because then it would “break” the web - even if the current reality can still be broken for those with disabilities. We should want to avoid stuff like that.</p> <p>But still, raise your issues. Make your requests. What else should popover reasonably be able to do? How should it be able to be controlled? And how will your proposal allow for a consistent accessible baseline? What is the line between a reasonable addition to popover’s functionality vs trying to make it into a different feature or element one might want?</p> <p>I don’t have all the answers to such questions - though I got opinions (sorry not sorry). But, I’m hopeful things will keep improving. I know everyone in Open UI, and in the web standards groups that end up defining these features want to do the right thing by all users. All I know is that I just want people to be mindful about what they ask for, and to not think that a feature that was meant to be an ingredient should instead be the main course.</p> ]]>

<title type="html">Paragraphs</title>
<link href="https://scottohara.me/blog/2024/08/29/paragraphs.html" rel="alternate" type="text/html" title="Paragraphs"/>
<published>2024-08-29T00:00:00+00:00</published>
<updated>2024-08-29T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
<id>https://scottohara.me/blog/2024/08/29/paragraphs</id>
<content type="html" xml:base="https://scottohara.me/blog/2024/08/29/paragraphs.html">
<![CDATA[ <p>Consider the following:</p> <p>I am a paragraph.</p> <p><span>I am also a paragraph.</span></p> <div>You might hate it, but I'm a paragraph too.</div> <ul> <li>Even I am a paragraph.</li> <li>Though I'm a list item as well.</li> </ul> <p>I might trick you</p> <address>Guess who? A paragraph!</address> <p>The above HTML-monologue is marked up as follows:</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><p></span>I am a paragraph.<span class="nt"></p></span> <span class="nt"><span></span>I am also a paragraph.<span class="nt"></span></span> <span class="nt"><div></span>You might hate it, but I'm a paragraph too.<span class="nt"></div></span> <span class="nt"><ul></span> <span class="nt"><li></span>Even I am a paragraph.<span class="nt"></li></span> <span class="nt"><li></span>Though I'm a list item as well.<span class="nt"></li></span> <span class="nt"></ul></span> <span class="nt"><p></span>I might trick you<span class="nt"></p></span> <span class="nt"><address></span>Guess who? A paragraph!<span class="nt"></address></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>You may look at that markup and say “Hey! You can’t fool me, only the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><p></code> elements are “real” paragraphs!</p> <p>You might even call out such elements as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code>s or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">span</code>s being used as “paragraphs” a WCAG failure.</p> <p>But, if you’re thinking those sorts of things, then maybe you’re not aware that those are <em>actually</em> all “paragraphs”.</p> <h2 id="what-you-talking-about-paragraph">What you talking about, paragraph?</h2> <p>In HTML there is the the <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/grouping-content.html#the-p-element"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> element</a>, which is the element you use if you want to explicitly markup text and other phrasing conetnt as a <em>paragraph</em>. But <strong>also</strong> in HTML, there is the more <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#paragraphs">general concept/definition of paragraphs</a>.</p> <p>I’m not going to just copy over all the text of the spec, you can read it at your leisure. Especially if you haven’t already <small>(don’t worry, lots of people - myself included - just start building stuff without reading the instructions first)</small>. But an example I want to highlight from the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> element section is as follows:</p> <blockquote> <p>List elements (in particular, ol and ul elements) cannot be children of p elements. When a sentence contains a bulleted list, therefore, one might wonder how it should be marked up.</p> <div class="example"> <p>For instance, this fantastic sentence has bullets relating to</p> <ul><li>wizards,</li> <li>faster-than-light travel, and</li> <li>telepathy,</li> </ul> <p> and is further discussed below.</p> </div> <p style="margin-top: 1.25em">The solution is to realize that a paragraph, in HTML terms, is not a logical concept, but a structural one. In the fantastic example above, there are actually five paragraphs as defined by this specification: one before the list, one for each bullet, and one after the list.</p> <p>The markup for the above example could therefore be:</p> <pre><code><p>For instance, this fantastic sentence has bullets relating to</p> <ul> <li>wizards, <li>faster-than-light travel, and <li>telepathy, </ul> <p>and is further discussed below.</p></code></pre> <p>Authors wishing to conveniently style such "logical" paragraphs consisting of multiple "structural" paragraphs can use the <code>div</code> element instead of the <code>p</code> element.</p> <p>Thus for instance the above example could become the following:</p> <pre><code><div>For instance, this fantastic sentence has bullets relating to <ul> <li>wizards, <li>faster-than-light travel, and <li>telepathy, </ul> and is further discussed below.</div></code></pre> <p>This example still has five structural paragraphs, but now the author can style just the div instead of having to consider each part of the example separately.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="isnt-the-p-element-important-for-screen-readers">Isn’t the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> element important for screen readers?</h2> <p>Testing one’s assumptions is a good thing. Please, do it more and often.</p> <p>Those examples I provided at the start of this post? macOS VoiceOver, NVDA, Narrator and JAWS treat them all as paragraphs (asterisks for NVDA, read on…)</p> <p>With VoiceOver, you can use the <kbd>VO</kbd> + <kbd>P</kbd> (paragraph/plain text) or <kbd>S</kbd> (same item) keys to navigate to each of the “paragraphs”. Similarly with JAWS, the <kbd>P</kbd> hot key navigates to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">li</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">span</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> paragraphs alike.</p> <p>NVDA behaves similarly, but at least with the latest version with the default settings on, they have some special logic in place where only the paragraph that have punctuation (e.g., a period) in them will be navigable by the <kbd>P</kbd> hot key. Without punctuation, they’re not navigated to… which I can only assume is to try and distinguish between legit paragraphs of content, and small incidental text that might just be a nuisance to navigate through. But, that’s just a guess.</p> <p>The point being that screen readers seem to be in step with HTML, at least from my understanding of what’s all going on here and actually testing how screen readers handle “paragraphs”. “Paragraphs” are more than just the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> element. That’s not an opinion, it’s how they’ve been defined in HTML for <em>years</em>. That’s not to say people should not use the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> element. It is absolutely the best practice when you need to define multiple blocks of paragraphs, rather than one <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code> full of a bunch of text with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">br</code> elements separating them. That’s just some sloppy slop. Writing explicitly semantic markup is often what people should aim for. It helps other developers understand your markup, it can be useful for styling, etc. etc. However, if you ever come across a “<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code> paragraph” in the wild, and your WCAG trigger finger starts itching… It might just be worth remembering all this and just leave it be. Apply some Benadryl. If you’re worried about how screen readers will handle it, test before you declare something’s broken and then look silly when it’s not. Not every paragraph <em>needs</em> to be a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> element with an implicit <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">paragraph</code> role.</p> <h2 id="well-then-why-the-aria-paragraph-role">Well, then why the ARIA <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">paragraph</code> role?</h2> <p>Oh damn it all… Fine, “good” question.</p> <p>It’s a role largely meant for parity with HTML elements. A role actually ‘needed’ by most web developers, is rather suspect.</p> <p>Similar to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">role=generic</code>. Don’t use it.</p> <p>Hell, if you even think you might want to try and get clever with it and do some things that HTML doesn’t allow, you’re probably setting yourself up for some foolishness.</p> <p>For instance, ever thought it’d be nice to try and include non-phrasing content (think things like figures, tables) in a “paragraph”? <small>(if so, need I remind you at this point of the HTML example I highlight above? but I digress..)</small> You can’t do that with standard <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> elements, because the HTML parser - rightly - is like “what the hell you think you’re doing?” And the following markup…</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><p></span> paragraph content goes here <span class="nt"><table></span><span class="c"><!-- table elements here --></span><span class="nt"></table></span> more content goes here <span class="nt"><ul></span><span class="c"><!-- list elements here --></span><span class="nt"></ul></span> last line of content here <span class="nt"></p></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>Gets rendered as:</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><p></span> paragraph content goes here <span class="nt"></p></span> <span class="nt"><table></span><span class="c"><!-- table elements here --></span><span class="nt"></table></span> more content goes here <span class="nt"><ul></span><span class="c"><!-- list elements here --></span><span class="nt"></ul></span> last line of content here <span class="nt"><p></p></span> <span class="c"><!-- lol --></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>Rare footage of the HTML parser at work...</p> <figure> <div style="position:relative"> <img src="/assets/img/p-parsing.gif" style="width: 100%;" alt="scene from ghostbusters where ray and egon fire their proton packs at a hotel cleaner pushing a cart, but in this gif the cart has the text 'p element' overlaid. The proton pack streams represent/have text saying 'lists, tables, you name it!'. When showing the cart being blasted by the proton packs, the text 'PARSING!!!!' is shown - representing the HTML parser attempting to make sense of the invalid content being thrown at it. The last scene shows the ghostbusters with text overlaid saying 'sorry. sorry. i thought we could just do whatever the hell we wanted'." id="gogo" /> <img src="/assets/img/parse-still.jpg" style="width:100%" alt="still of the animated gif with the large text 'parsing' appearing" id="stopped" hidden="" /> <button aria-pressed="false" id="ppb" style="position: absolute; bottom: 0; right: 0;">Stop animated gif</button> </div> <figcaption> <p>The HTML parser will exclaim "what the hell you doing?" if you try to nest invalid children into a paragraph element.</p> <p>For anyone unfamiliar with the scene from Ghostbusters that I made that gif from, <a href="https://youtu.be/ZJVgfDnjkko?si=iC-7rMlBxLXq5Uqn&t=43">here is the scene on YouTube</a>.</p> </figcaption> </figure> <script> const ani = document.getElementById('gogo'); const stpd = document.getElementById('stopped'); const ppb = document.getElementById('ppb'); ppb.addEventListener('click', ()=> { if ( ppb.getAttribute('aria-pressed') === 'false' ) { ppb.setAttribute('aria-pressed', 'true'); stpd.hidden = false; ani.hidden = true; } else { ppb.setAttribute('aria-pressed', 'false'); stpd.hidden = true; ani.hidden = false; } }); </script> <h3 id="but-what-about-aria--aria-does-what-htmldont">But, what about ARIA? <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k7nsBoqJ6s8">ARIA does what HTMLdon’t</a>.</h3> <p>Why not try and get around the awkwardness of proton pack p-parsing, and do something like the following?</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><div</span> <span class="na">role=</span><span class="s">paragraph</span><span class="nt">></span> p is for paragraph but that's not good enough for me <span class="nt"><table></span><span class="c"><!-- table elements here --></span><span class="nt"></table></span> i want a table inside of my gosh darn p <span class="nt"><ul></span><span class="c"><!-- list elements here --></span><span class="nt"></ul></span> maybe a list too, that'd fill me with some semantic glee, oh, paragraph is spelled 'd i v r o l e = p a r a g r a p h' <span class="nt"></div></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>Really rolls off the muppet’s tongue, doesn’t it?</p> <p>The problem with the above, and the thinking behind it, is that it doesn’t do anything useful.</p> <p>Where it works best, someone using a screen reader wouldn’t notice any difference to whether the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">role=paragraph</code> was used, or if it was rendered as the parsed HTML of the prior example. The insertion of the tables, lists, whatever - those container elements are still <em>not</em> paragraphs, and thus they’d still result in a necessary distinction from the screen reader reading a string of text / phrasing content, to then encountering a block of content which is <em>not just</em> a string of text / phrasing content.</p> <p>Additionally, just quickly testing with the latest versions/browsers of screen readers (available at the time of writing), some oddities with the above get introduced <small>(maybe you saw that coming. Misusing ARIA to try n’ all)</small>. For instance, if specifically using paragraph navigation (the <kbd>P</kbd> hot key) JAWS would skip over the first line of the ‘paragraph’ and just start reading all the content of the table’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">thead</code> as a string, no table semantics to speak of. Or, if attempting to navigate by tables on with the iOS rotor, there’d be ‘none’ to find.</p> <p>Again I will note that generally speaking, doing something like this doesn’t immediately impact someone’s ability to read the content. It’s when using specific screen reader commands that things could get a bit messy. Just repeating myself as I anticipate someone reading the above and being like “Scott says this breaks the internet!” and jeezy-creezy, I did not friggin say that…</p> <h2 id="was-there-a-point-to-all-of-this">Was there a point to all of this?</h2> <p>Yes.</p> <p>Focus on markup issues/problems that actually have a detrimental impact on users. Futzing about whether to use a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">span</code> vs a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> element as the most semantic tag for content that is already covered under the umbrella of “paragraphs” is generally not one of them, in my opinion. Sigh… I just realized this entire blog post is just an elongated version of what I <a href="https://www.scottohara.me/blog/2022/01/20/divisive.html#the-severity-of-semantics">already covered in my post about <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code>s from 2022</a>. So much for being new and interesting?</p> <p>Also, a reminder to test your assumptions. Don’t just assume the use of a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code> is a bad thing (see again my <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code> post), or that you can slap-dash ARIA on whatever you want and somehow make it better without actually verifying that to be true or not. The over use of ARIA has taught LLM AI some pretty ridiculous bad practices that now need to be untaught. It’s annoying.</p> <p>Also, <em>also</em>, I wanted to make silly 80s pop culture references, and the best way I can think to do that is through some snarky educational content. So I did.</p> <p>After all, I ain’t charging for this shit. :)</p> <p>The end.</p> ]]>

<title type="html">Spoiler Alert: it needs to be accessible</title>
<link href="https://scottohara.me/blog/2024/08/22/spoiler.html" rel="alternate" type="text/html" title="Spoiler Alert: it needs to be accessible"/>
<published>2024-08-22T00:00:00+00:00</published>
<updated>2024-08-22T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
<id>https://scottohara.me/blog/2024/08/22/spoiler</id>
<content type="html" xml:base="https://scottohara.me/blog/2024/08/22/spoiler.html">
<![CDATA[ <p>The topic of how to make an accessible spoiler component, or ‘should there be a spoiler element?’ has recently (re)-caught my attention. <small>(I wrote most of this back in February and then forgot about it… as I seem to do these days. But then people necro’d a GitHub issue on the topic, so here we go again)</small></p> <p>Now, I could do what I usually do and write some long winded junk about what a spoiler is, how it’s essentially a glorified disclosure widget… maybe mention something about the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">details</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">summary</code> elements and how they likely wouldn’t be sufficient for all use cases. Blah blah blah. Boring.</p> <p>Instead, I’m just going to tell you what I’d expect from a spoiler component if someone were to build one, or if one were to ever be standardized. I’ll try to keep it as short as I possibly can (which I’m bad at).</p> <h2 id="spoiler-1-there-needs-to-be-a-semantic-container-element">Spoiler 1: there needs to be a semantic container element</h2> <p>While one obviously needs some sort of container to delineate the content that needs to be marked as spoilery - it can’t just be a plain old <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code>. Insert your bewildered ‘gasps’ here.</p> <p>Someone using a screen reader, for instance, needs to be able to know that they’ve entered a section of content that represents spoiler material, and also importantly, when they’ve reached the end of such content.</p> <p>We should also be mindful to the fact that spoilers can represent an entire section of content, which could contain multiple paragraphs / structured content (e.g., lists n’ such). Or, it could be a string of text within a paragraph.</p> <p>In lieu of a standardized element with a <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#transparent-content-models">transparent content model</a> (see how <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">del</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ins</code> work / allow for otherwise ‘invalid’ nesting, if you aren’t sure what that term means), the spoiler container will need to be a custom element so we don’t need to switch between a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code> and a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">span</code> (the latter being able to be used within a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">p</code> element, where the former would cause the browser’s parser to kick it out).</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><spoiler-component></span> ... <span class="nt"></spoiler-component></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>As far as default accessibility semantics are concerned, a custom element is a long-winded way to write <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">span</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">div</code>, and that won’t cut it. So we need to give this thing a role and an accessible name to help define those boundaries I mentioned.</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><spoiler-component</span> <span class="na">aria-label=</span><span class="s">"Spoiler"</span> <span class="na">role=</span><span class="s">"group"</span><span class="nt">></span> ... <span class="nt"></spoiler-component></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>With this in place, we now have a wrapper to define the boundaries of the spoiler content. It will be exposed as a ‘group’ with the name of ‘spoiler’, identifying that any content within this group is spoiler-related. (please note that <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">group</code> might not be the ‘best’ role for this… but also, in my opinion there is presently no better role, so here we are)</p> <h2 id="spoiler-2-there-needs-to-be-a-way-for-it-to-be-accessed-by-non-pointer-mouse-inputs">Spoiler 2: there needs to be a way for it to be accessed by non-pointer (mouse) inputs</h2> <p>If you think that someone should be able to reveal the spoiler content by clicking anywhere on this element, then sure. That can happen. But, you can’t stop thinking there - sorry, I know thinking is hard.</p> <p>We need a way for someone who isn’t using a pointer device (mouse, touch, etc.) to be able to reveal the spoiler content. So what are we to do? We add a keyboard accessible control to provide this function. You might have heard of “buttons”?</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><spoiler-component</span> <span class="na">aria-label=</span><span class="s">"Spoiler"</span> <span class="na">role=</span><span class="s">"group"</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><button></span>Reveal Spoiler<span class="nt"></button></span> ... <span class="nt"></spoiler-component></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>Now we have a keyboard accessible way to reach this spoiler content. <strong>But also</strong> the visible button text helps identify why this blurred or blocked out content is presented this way. Cause you know… spoilery, content or ‘gated/potentially nsfw’ content can look similar in their visual treatment (visually obscured but still takes up space in the document flow). But they actually represent very different things… almost like just because some things look similar, you can’t just assume they’re the same… if this was Twitter, I’d be subtweeting really hard right now.</p> <p>While we’re at it though, it <em>should</em> be a default that someone can show/hide (a.k.a., ‘toggle’ - it’s an industry term) the spoiler content. And that’s for a few reasons:</p> <ol> <li>It might not be desired for the content to remain visible. We don’t know what the spoiler content could be, and maybe there’s something that gets displayed that one doesn’t always want to be displayed? Use your imagination… People should have a way to hide this content again if they want/need to.</li> <li>If the button goes away when the spoiler content is shown, then we have to worry about focus management. Otherwise, as often happens when people don’t think about this, a screen reader’s virtual cursor could find itself sent back to the start of the web page, and that user would then need to re-navigate the page to find the content again - but this time without the ability to navigate to the button with the name of ‘spoiler’.</li> <li>Keeping the button in place also allows us to provide a confirmation of action to the user by using an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">aria-expanded</code> attribute. When first encountering the button, someone using a screen reader will hear the button is in the “collapsed” state. And activating it will announce it in an “expanded” state, thus signaling the button actually did what it was supposed to do, and now they can go spoil themselves.</li> </ol> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><spoiler-component</span> <span class="na">aria-label=</span><span class="s">"Spoiler"</span> <span class="na">role=</span><span class="s">"group"</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><button</span> <span class="na">aria-expanded=</span><span class="s">"true|false"</span><span class="nt">></span>Reveal Spoiler<span class="nt"></button></span> ... <span class="nt"></spoiler-component></span> </code></pre></div></div> <h2 id="spoiler-3-gotta-actually-hide-the-spoiler-content-to-everyone">Spoiler 3: gotta actually hide the spoiler content <em>to everyone</em></h2> <p>We can’t just blur, block or blot out the spoiler content <small>(I don’t actually know what a blotting treatment would visually entail here, but it was a 3rd ‘b’ word for obscuring content, so I’m keeping it there. Why am I explaining this to you?)</small>.</p> <p>There are two bits we need to consider here:</p> <ol> <li>Visual styles alone won’t make the content actually hidden. Someone using their mouse could still copy the visually obscured content, or someone using a screen reader could still access the content. Additionally, if there are nested keyboard focusable elements within the spoiler, then those too could still be reached by someone navigating by keyboard. None of that’s what we want.</li> <li>Since the “Spoiler” toggle button needs to be inside of the “Spoiler” <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">group</code>, we can’t blanket obscure everything within it.</li> </ol> <p>So we can adjust the markup by adding a nested container as a sibling for the button. We can also use the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">inert</code> attribute to serve as our styling hook, which also makes sure the content can’t be accessed when its obscured.</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><spoiler-component</span> <span class="na">aria-label=</span><span class="s">"Spoiler"</span> <span class="na">role=</span><span class="s">"group"</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><button</span> <span class="na">aria-expanded=</span><span class="s">"false"</span><span class="nt">></span>Reveal Spoiler<span class="nt"></button></span> <span class="nt"><spoiler-content</span> <span class="na">inert</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="c"><!-- look, it's inert! --></span> ... <span class="nt"></spoiler-component></span> <span class="nt"></spoiler-content></span> </code></pre></div></div> <div role="note"> <p>One problem with this idea right now is that <code>inert</code> content can still be found when using a browser's "find" feature (e.g., <kbd>ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>F</kbd>). My feelings on whether inert content should be 'found' are complicated... But I'm trying to keep this short. So moving on.</p> </div> <h2 id="spoiler-4-but-howzitwork">Spoiler 4: But howzitwork?</h2> <p>Well, I made a fancy-dancy (it is neither of those) CodePen to show you. The JavaScript is slapdash, the CSS is incredibly basic. I’m sure you can do better. Don’t @ me. I don’t care.</p> <p class="codepen" data-height="448" data-default-tab="html,result" data-slug-hash="xxBagPy" data-user="scottohara" style="height: 448px; box-sizing: border-box; display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; border: 2px solid; margin: 1em 0; padding: 1em;"> <span>See the Pen <a href="https://codepen.io/scottohara/pen/xxBagPy"> Spoiler Component</a> by Scott (<a href="https://codepen.io/scottohara">@scottohara</a>) on <a href="https://codepen.io">CodePen</a>.</span> </p> <script async="" src="https://cpwebassets.codepen.io/assets/embed/ei.js"></script> <h3 id="but-you-keep-the-button-visible-at-all-times-i-dont-want-that">But you keep the button visible at all times!? I don’t want that!</h3> <p>Yup. I’m sorry you don’t want that. I don’t want to remove or hide it.</p> <p>I’m sure a compromise can be made. But the button really should be persistently available so that people can toggle the content, and so that one doesn’t need to worry about moving focus when the button ‘disappears’ on them after activating.</p> <p>Might someone decide to visually hide their button? Sure… I’m not going to fight ya on that, so long as it still works for all your users. But, if one were to standardize this, the default should be as accessible by default as possible. And that probably means the button should be persistent by default.</p> <h2 id="wrap-it-up">Wrap it up</h2> <p>A standardized accessible component like this <em>could</em> be useful for more than just temporarily hiding the key plot points of a [ insert thing you want to spoil here ]. Arguably it could be a useful component to have for interfaces that need to edit or present documents where content needs to be obscured.</p> <p>Additinoally, a standardized component could provide a simplified aural UI in ways that are arguably a bit cumbersome for a web developer to deliver on.</p> <p>For instance, rather than a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">group</code> with the name of “spoiler” - a new variant of a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">group</code> role could be created, with a localized role description (a.k.a., the ‘name’ of the role) of “spoiler” or “obscured” or something else… So instead of needing to name a generic group, you could just have an element that was announced with the name of that role.</p> <p>There are other things that a browser implementation could consider - from exactly how to handle the inert content (making sure it can’t be found by the browser find feature), or even how it might handle the button part / focusability of the element in general. Maybe a browser-implementation could even go to the point of removing the spoiler/redacted content form the source code? I dunno about that… but you can’t <em>really</em> have truly redacted content on the web if you can just few source to check it out, can you?</p> <p>My example is merely demonstrating a basic styled example of what I’d expect this to look like based on what can be done as a web author.</p> <p>Ok, fun. This wasn’t too long, I guess.</p> ]]>

<title type="html">The search element</title>
<link href="https://scottohara.me/blog/2023/03/24/search-element.html" rel="alternate" type="text/html" title="The search element"/>
<published>2023-03-24T00:00:00+00:00</published>
<updated>2023-03-24T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
<id>https://scottohara.me/blog/2023/03/24/search-element</id>
<content type="html" xml:base="https://scottohara.me/blog/2023/03/24/search-element.html">
<![CDATA[ <p>Today, March 24th 2023, the HTML specification added a new grouping content element. The <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/grouping-content.html#the-search-element"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search</code> element</a>.</p> <div role="note"> <p>Please be aware that this element landing in the HTML spec today <strong>does not mean it is available in browsers today</strong>. Issues have been filed to implement the <code>search</code> element in the major browsers, including the necessary accessibility mappings. Keep this in mind when you add this new element to your pages.</p> <p>Support update: Safari 17, Firefox 118 and Chrome/Edge 118 support the `search` element mapping to the implicit `search` landmark role. Safari 17 released mid September, Firefox early October and Chromium browsers will update to 118 during October, as well.</p> </div> <p>The impetus for this addition stems from the <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5811">“Consider creating an HTML search element” issue</a>, filed on the HTML spec in late 2020, where the goal was to create feature parity between ARIA and HTML.</p> <p>ARIA defines <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#landmark_roles">8 landmark roles</a> to help authors structure their web pages. For every landmark role, except for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search</code>, a native HTML element could be used - under certain conditions - to expose these landmark roles. BTW, I’ve written a few things about landmarks in the past. Here’s but one of them <a href="https://www.scottohara.me/blog/2018/03/03/landmarks.html">Accessible Landmarks</a>.</p> <p>With the addition of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search</code>, now every ARIA landmark has a native HTML equivalent. And also, now everyone who has ever written about ARIA landmarks needs to go update their articles. Have fun! <small>(I’m going to update mine later. Don’t @ or DM me.)</small></p> <h2 id="how-to-use-it">How to use it</h2> <p>First and foremost, one would use the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search</code> element to expose the search landmark in the browser’s accessibility API, allowing people using assistive technology, such as screen readers, to discover this content area and allow for quick access to it. Being a “search” landmark, it implicitly indicates that the content one would find within would be related to searching for, or even filtering content (filtering is a ‘searching’ behavior… designers sure do like to use the magnify glass icon interchangeably between these UI controls, at least).</p> <p>Very on the nose, but that’s the point.</p> <p>Typically a search landmark will contain, at minimum, a text field (either identified as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">input type=text</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">type=search</code> - <a href="https://adrianroselli.com/2019/07/ignore-typesearch.html">read this if you’re wondering why one wouldn’t necessarily default to just <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">type=search</code></a>). Additionally, but not necessarily, a button to initiate the search would be another expected descendant of the landmark. Finally, other form controls, descriptive content or links related to understanding or modifying one’s search or filtering query could be present. E.g., checkboxes or radio buttons to modify the parameters.</p> <p>Markup for a simple search where JavaScript is used to initiate the search functionality:</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><search></span> <span class="nt"><label</span> <span class="na">for=</span><span class="s">s</span><span class="nt">></span>Site<span class="nt"></label></span> <span class="nt"><input</span> <span class="na">type=</span><span class="s">search</span> <span class="na">id=</span><span class="s">s</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><button></span>Go!<span class="nt"></button></span> <span class="nt"></search></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>Markup for a simple search where a traditional form submission is used for the search functionality:</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><search></span> <span class="nt"><form</span> <span class="na">action=</span><span class="s">"search.php"</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><label</span> <span class="na">for=</span><span class="s">"query"</span><span class="nt">></span>Find an article<span class="nt"></label></span> <span class="nt"><input</span> <span class="na">id=</span><span class="s">"query"</span> <span class="na">name=</span><span class="s">"q"</span> <span class="na">type=</span><span class="s">"search"</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><button</span> <span class="na">type=</span><span class="s">"submit"</span><span class="nt">></span>Go!<span class="nt"></button></span> <span class="nt"></form></span> <span class="nt"></search></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>Some <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/grouping-content.html#the-search-element">additional reduced markup <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search</code> patterns</a> can be found in the examples of the HTML spec element definition.</p> <h3 id="why-would-i-use-this-instead-of-form-rolesearch">Why would I use this instead of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">form role=search</code></h3> <p>You might be looking at that second example, where a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">form</code> element is nested within the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search</code> element and think “huh… a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search</code> element would still need a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">form</code>? That seems like extra work to use two elements.”</p> <p>And sure, that’s a valid takeaway. Two elements <em>is more than one</em> and you can identify a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">form</code> element as a search landmark now by adding a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">role=search</code> to it. But when has extra work ever stopped a web developer?</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><div</span> <span class="na">role=</span><span class="s">button</span> <span class="na">tabindex=</span><span class="s">0</span><span class="nt">></span> Sure i could use the button element, but F that noise. <span class="nt"></div></span> <span class="c"><!-- F stands for "forget", obviously... --></span> <span class="nt"><script></span> <span class="cm">/* all the necessary keyboard interactions and behaviors that now must be recreated to make an accessible "button" */</span> <span class="nt"></script></span> <span class="nt"><style></span> <span class="c">/* all the styles for the default button state, disabled, hovered, focused, high contrast mode styles, anything else i'm currently forgetting... have fun recreating the wheel, yo :) */</span> <span class="nt"></style></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>But seriously, there was quite a bit of back and forth on whether the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search</code> element should be another type of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">form</code>, but there was no appetite to do this from the browser implementers (for very reasonable reasons, mind you), and honestly, it is not that big of a deal.</p> <p>The goal of the element proposal was to provide landmark parity with the available ARIA roles. The element achieves this, and everyone is still perfectly entitled to use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><form role=search></code> for where that would be appropriate. But now, you also <em>don’t have to use ARIA</em>, which is also one of the driving principles of ARIA. As the ARIA spec mentions a few times (the following two quotes taken from different parts of the spec):</p> <blockquote> <p>When the host language provides a feature that provides equivalent accessibility to the WAI-ARIA feature, use the host language feature.<br /> …<br /> When a feature in the host language with identical role semantics and values is available, and the author has no compelling reason to avoid using the host language feature, authors SHOULD use the host language features rather than repurpose other elements with WAI-ARIA.</p> </blockquote> <p>So, for all you JavaScript developers out there who need to implement a search feature and should be exposing it as a landmark but have no practical use for native <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">form</code> behaviors, this one’s for you.</p> <div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><search>...</search> vs <div role=search>...</div> </code></pre></div></div> <p>17 vs 23 characters. You’re welcome.</p> <h2 id="a-final-thought-and-thank-you">A final thought and thank you</h2> <p>To be brutally honest, this is not the most important element that’s ever been added to the HTML specification. It <em>is</em> however a nice little accessibility win. People don’t <em>have to</em> use ARIA to get this feature. It fills a little hole that has always been present, and every little bit helps.</p> <p>Additionally, it was a very good experience getting to work on this with the HTML editors (primarily <a href="https://twitter.com/domenic">@domenic </a>, who helped me with getting the PR done) and fellow ARIA working group member, <a href="https://twitter.com/carmacleod">Carolyn MacLeod</a> who originally made the proposal to HTML to add this element. Further discussing this new element with browser implementers, and identifying a need for some HTML parsing updates (which will be important with other new features coming to HTML) was an interesting, related bit to this process. Maybe more on that another time.</p> <p>Also, if you’re interested in getting involved with working on the ARIA specification, here’s a nice and easy entry issue to reference the new <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search</code> element to get you going: <a href="https://github.com/w3c/aria/issues/1898">ARIA issue #1898 - Add base concept for search role</a>.</p> <p>But finally, Carolyn unfortunately passed away in February of 2022. This was the last thing I was able to work on with her. Again, while not the biggest win for the accessibility community, I know seeing what she started finally get merged into the spec would have made her happy.</p> <p>So, I’m really glad this element is now part of HTML, and will soon be available for people to use to markup their web pages. Thanks Carolyn for helping to make this happen.</p> ]]>
