<title type="html">Use the dialog element (reasonably)</title>
<link href="https://scottohara.me/blog/2023/01/26/use-the-dialog-element.html" rel="alternate" type="text/html" title="Use the dialog element (reasonably)"/>
<published>2023-01-26T00:00:00+00:00</published>
<updated>2023-01-26T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
<id>https://scottohara.me/blog/2023/01/26/use-the-dialog-element</id>
<content type="html" xml:base="https://scottohara.me/blog/2023/01/26/use-the-dialog-element.html">
<![CDATA[ <p>Today, the HTML specification landed a <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/a9f103c9f7bd09ef712990194638c75db1f50e3c">very important change to the dialog element</a>. One that resolves a multi-year discussion on how the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element should handle initial focus.</p> <p>As mentioned in the linked PR, the specific changes here are to:</p> <ol> <li>Make the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> focusing steps look at sequentially focusable elements instead of any focusable element.</li> <li>Make the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element itself get focus if it has the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">autofocus</code> attribute set.</li> <li>Make the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element itself get focus as a fallback instead of focus being reset to the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">body</code> element.</li> </ol> <p>As this has just landed, it will take a bit more time for any of these changes (in the cases where they were not already implemented) to appear in browsers. But this is a good day for the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element.</p> <p>As mentioned in the PR, <strong>there are still additional topics that need to be discussed and worked on</strong>. But, that’s also true for many HTML features. HTML is not perfect. That’s not a dig. Nothing’s perfect. And that’s why HTML, and other specifications, are constantly being worked on.</p> <p>Instead of waiting for perfect, I <em>personally</em> think it’s time to move away from using custom dialogs, and to use the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element instead.</p> <h2 id="use-it">Use it</h2> <p><em>IMO</em>, the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element has reached the tipping point of <em>generally</em> being the better option for web developers who need to implement dialogs in their web pages. The number of accessibility requirements a developer needs to be aware of, and the level of effort to implement custom ARIA dialogs is now largely taken care of by browsers.</p> <p>Will you still have use cases that would require a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">role=dialog</code> over a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element? Yes.</p> <p>Does your website or web application have its own requirements (user base, need to support legacy browsers, limited time/resources) that would make it unreasonable to migrate to using the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element? Sure!</p> <p>But, if those - or other unmentioned reasons - don’t apply. Then it seems you’re a prime candidate to use the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element, with a minimal amount of JavaScript to implement. Versus adding an additional dependency (even if that <a href="https://github.com/KittyGiraudel/a11y-dialog">dependency is pretty darn great</a>), or deciding that someone else’s code doesn’t smell like you, so, let’s reinvent the wheel, again!</p> <h2 id="dont-abuse-it">Don’t abuse it</h2> <p>Now, let’s not get <a href="https://modalzmodalzmodalz.com/">reckless with dialogs</a>. This isn’t really advice that’s unique to the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> element itself. People have a long history of taking elements/components that were intended for specific use cases, and then stressing them to their limit to fit <em>their</em> use case. Sometimes this makes sense, but other times (e.g., when your modal dialog consists of various headings, landmarks, and long-form content) it’s maybe best to sit back, take a deep breath, and think to yourself:</p> <blockquote> <p>Self. Hey. It's me, you know... you. I'm wondering. Maybe, just <em>maybe</em> we <strong>don't</strong> need to shove a web page into another web page by use of a smaller window atop the first web page.</p> <p>...</p> <p>I mean, we are already using an SPA. So ostensibly, even the argument that we need to use a modal dialog to save state, rather than going to a new web page, is a garbage lie we tell ourselves to maintain the way we've always done things, rather than accept the reality that we're absolutely willing to change course on other design and technical decisions due to a change in the wind from an opinionated topic within our community...</p> <p>...</p> <p>Oh F it, of course we need to keep shoving web pages into web pages! LOLOLOL! I LOVE MY DECISIONS!</p> </blockquote> <p>Well, that conversation didn’t go the way I had hoped… Anyway, yeh. Just because it’s easier to make dialogs now, than it has ever been, just please check yourself.</p> <h2 id="report-issues--bugs">Report issues / bugs!</h2> <p>To round this out, I’ll again make mention that there are still aspects of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> which need work, or may even need to be implemented at all. For instance, non-modal (or modeless) dialogs? There’s some big question marks on how exactly that type of dialog should behave.</p> <p>But, the best way to find out where there are still issues (functional, accessibility specific, feature requests, etc.) is to give the element a proper “go”.</p> <p>So give the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">dialog</code> a try. Be purposeful and reasonable with its use, keeping in mind any additional requirements that may limit or necessitate further testing and research (user, a11y, other) on your end.</p> <p>Now if you’ll excuse me. I want to take a break from talking about dialogs for awhile (or at least, until its relevant to do so again) :)</p> ]]>

<title type="html">Responsive accessibility using visibility hidden</title>
<link href="https://scottohara.me/blog/2022/11/07/responsive-accessibility.html" rel="alternate" type="text/html" title="Responsive accessibility using visibility hidden"/>
<published>2022-11-07T00:00:00+00:00</published>
<updated>2022-11-07T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
<id>https://scottohara.me/blog/2022/11/07/responsive-accessibility</id>
<content type="html" xml:base="https://scottohara.me/blog/2022/11/07/responsive-accessibility.html">
<![CDATA[ <p>Like it or not, even though content can be made to adapt to different viewport sizes and zoom levels by use of CSS media queries, sometimes the end result can be a bit awkward without further adjustments that go beyond visual presentation.</p> <p>Without getting too into it, sometimes content that may appear in the normal flow of a web page may need to instead be rendered as a dialog on smaller viewports. Or, UI which shows/hides may make sense on smaller viewports but does not need to be treated this way when a larger viewport is available.</p> <p>While HTML provides features, such as the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">source</code> element’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">media</code> attribute, where the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">source</code> for a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">picture</code> element will be determined based on a media query breakpoint, this capability doesn’t extend to other HTML elements.</p> <p>Maybe something like it should?</p> <p>I have a few use cases for this, but let’s just look at one for now.</p> <h2 id="media-queries-to-toggle-toggles">Media queries to toggle toggles</h2> <p>Imagine you have an FAQ page where on large screen all the commonly asked questions which unfortunately are not obvious enough to figure out are fully displayed with their answers for people to read. On small screen, however, in an effort to help someone be able to find the question they want answered with a reduced amount of scrolling, all the answers have been collapsed by default.</p> <p>So on large screen we have a web page that is a series of headings followed by their answers, which would have a markup pattern like so:</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><h</span><span class="na">#</span><span class="nt">></span> Frequently asked question <span class="nt"></h</span><span class="err">#</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><div></span>Answer goes here!<span class="nt"></div></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>But on small screen, a pattern like the following would be expected:</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><h</span><span class="na">#</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><button</span> <span class="na">aria-expanded=</span><span class="s">"..."</span><span class="nt">></span>Frequently asked question<span class="nt"></button></span> <span class="nt"></h</span><span class="err">#</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><div></span>Answer goes here!<span class="nt"></div></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>Now, we don’t want to have to redo the DOM depending on the viewport size. That’d be annoying. We also can’t just style away the visual presentation of the button on larger screens, because the underlying implicit and explicit ARIA semantics would still be exposed to people using assistive technology. And, the button functionality and focusability would still remain, regardless of styling.</p> <p>Again, one might think to use JavaScript to potentially add/remove the button based on viewport size. Or, maybe because that’s super annoying, one could add remove ARIA and HTML attributes to the button(s) to suppress the semantics and behaviors. But that too would be annoying and you’d end up with some garbage markup at large screen that resembled the following:</p> <div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><h#> <button aria-expanded="..." disabled role="none" >Frequently asked question</button> </h#> <div>Answer goes here!</div> </code></pre></div></div> <p>Where the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">disabled</code> attribute would need to be applied to completely suppress the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> element’s focusability (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">tabindex=-1</code> would only remove it from the focus order of the page, but would still mean it was focusable, after all). Styling would need to be done to make the now <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">disabled</code> button not <em>look</em> disabled. The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">role=none</code> would then need to be applied to the button so that its implicit button role and disabled state were no longer communicated.</p> <p>That’s annoying and even though it’s not adding and removing a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> element, it is potentially a lot of DOM manipulation.</p> <h3 id="using-css-and-visibility">Using CSS and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">visibility</code></h3> <p>Instead of modifying the DOM, we could instead write the some CSS to show/hide the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> element based on the necessary media query breakpoints.</p> <p>Consider the following:</p> <div class="language-html highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nt"><h3></span> <span class="nt"><button</span> <span class="na">aria-expanded=</span><span class="s">...</span><span class="nt">></span> <span class="nt"><span></span>My text<span class="nt"></span></span> <span class="nt"></button></span> <span class="nt"></h3></span> <span class="nt"><div</span> <span class="na">class=</span><span class="s">content</span><span class="nt">></span> the content that toggles depending on breakpoint. <span class="nt"></div></span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>Not too different than the small screen markup needed for setting up the disclosure widgets, but here there’s a new <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">span</code> element that contains the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> element’s content. Why?</p> <p>Well, this is where <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/web/css/visibility">CSS’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">visibility</code> property</a> comes into play.</p> <p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">visibility</code> property is an interesting one. When applied to an element with the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hidden</code> value, it will result in the element and its contents being visually hidden, though it still takes up the “space” that it would in the rendered web page. It’s just like one big visual hole and is similar to if you had applied <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">opacity: 0</code> to that same content. However, unlike with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">opacity</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">visibility: hidden</code> will result in that content <strong>not</strong> being exposed by the browser’s accessibility API (i.e., it won’t show up in the a11y tree). This is similar behavior to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">display: none</code> which also hides content from the a11y tree.</p> <p>What makes <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">visibility</code> even more different, and <em>useful</em> here, is that you can make parts of a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">visibility: hidden</code> subtree visible again.</p> <p>Let’s now look at this in context of the markup pattern for the FAQ show/hide buttons.</p> <p>At large screen viewports the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> element needs to be hidden. But, the text within needs to be visible at all viewports. So if we were do to the following:</p> <div class="language-css highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">@media</span> <span class="n">screen</span> <span class="n">and</span> <span class="p">(</span> <span class="n">min-width</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="m">600px</span> <span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="nt">button</span><span class="o">[</span><span class="nt">aria-expanded</span><span class="o">]</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="nl">visibility</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nb">hidden</span><span class="p">;</span> <span class="p">}</span> <span class="p">}</span> <span class="nt">button</span><span class="o">[</span><span class="nt">aria-expanded</span><span class="o">]</span> <span class="nt">span</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="nl">visibility</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nb">visible</span><span class="p">;</span> <span class="p">}</span> </code></pre></div></div> <p>The first ruleset within the media query will ensure that the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> elements with the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">aria-expanded</code> attribute will be hidden at viewport sizes larger than 600px. Ensuring that the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> element will not be exposed.</p> <p>The second ruleset will ensure that the subtree of the button, contained within the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">span</code> element, will always be shown regardless of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">button</code> element being set to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">visibility: hidden</code> or not.</p> <p>With some additional styles and JavaScript to properly setup the disclosure widget (hey, <a href="https://www.scottohara.me/blog/2022/09/12/details-summary.html#creating-an-aria-disclosure-widget">I wrote something about that</a>), you can get the following:</p> <p class="codepen" data-height="300" data-default-tab="html,result" data-slug-hash="abKBvMP" data-user="scottohara" style="height: 300px; box-sizing: border-box; display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; border: 2px solid; margin: 1em 0; padding: 1em;"> <span>See the Pen <a href="https://codepen.io/scottohara/pen/abKBvMP"> responsive toggle button</a> by Scott (<a href="https://codepen.io/scottohara">@scottohara</a>) on <a href="https://codepen.io">CodePen</a>.</span> </p> <script async="" src="https://cpwebassets.codepen.io/assets/embed/ei.js"></script> <h2 id="isnt-this-a-little-hacky--confusing-though">Isn’t this a little hacky / confusing though?</h2> <p>It sure is. But right now we don’t have a particularly good solution to do this without leaning too heavily on JavaScript or potentially even CSS to do things that really probably belong as a native HTML feature so that stuff like this can even work if JavaScript or CSS are not available. E.g., when these extra resources are blocked or fail to load for some reason or another. Whether that be through a problem with the server, or someone purposefully turning on reader mode for their browser and all author defined CSS and JS are kicked to the curb.</p> <p>Extra effort would need to be taken (likely with JavaScript) to make this behave in a nice progressively enhanced sort of way. But, I’m content with just being clever today. Maybe I, or someone else, can figure out how to make this a smart idea some other time.</p> ]]>
